lead: A metal holds a gas of electrons free to move between fixed positive ions. A field accelerates them; collisions stop them, so they settle into a slow steady drift. This balance gives Ohm's law and conductivity σ = ne²τ/m. Drude proposed this around 1900. It explains why a copper wire obeys V = IR and why nichrome makes a good heater coil. It also fails in clear ways that point to quantum theory.
prereq: You need current, current density, drift velocity and electric field from Unit 3, and force and energy from Unit 1.

sections.h3: A metal as a gas of free electrons

blocks.text: A metal is a lattice of fixed positive ions with conduction electrons moving between them. The outermost electrons leave their atoms and belong to the whole solid; they carry current. Drude used a gas-in-a-box analogy.
The model rests on four assumptions:

items: Free: between collisions an electron feels no force from the ions or from other electrons.
Random motion: velocities point in all directions, so the average velocity is zero when no field is applied.
Collisions: an electron strikes an ion after an average time τ, the relaxation time, and forgets the velocity gained. For a metal at room temperature τ is of order 10⁻¹⁴ s.

blocks.text: The symbol n is the number density of conduction electrons: free electrons per cubic metre. For copper, n = 8.5×10²⁸ m⁻³, roughly one free electron per atom. The model computes σ from these microscopic numbers.

sections.h3: Drift velocity, mobility and the relaxation time

blocks.text: Field E gives force F = eE and acceleration a = eE/m, with e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C and m = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg. Without collisions the current would grow forever; collisions prevent that.
An electron just after a collision gains speed eEt/m in a flight of duration t. Averaging flights with mean τ gives a small steady drift opposite E for the negative electron:
v_d = eEτ/m   and   μ = v_d/E = eτ/m
blocks.where: v_d is drift velocity in m/s; e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C; E is field in V/m; τ is relaxation time in s; m = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg; μ is mobility in m²/(V·s).

blocks.text: For copper with τ = 2.5×10⁻¹⁴ s, μ = (1.6×10⁻¹⁹)(2.5×10⁻¹⁴)/(9.11×10⁻³¹) ≈ 4.4×10⁻³ m²/(V·s). Drift is slow; it sits on top of fast random motion.
Current density is charge crossing unit area per second. With n electrons per cubic metre, each drifting at v_d, the charge crossing one square metre per second is nev_d.

blocks.where: J is current density in A/m²; n is electron density in m⁻³; v_d is drift velocity in m/s; σ is conductivity in S/m; ρ = 1/σ = m/(ne²τ) is resistivity in Ω·m.

blocks.text: This is Ohm's law at the microscopic level. It is linear because v_d is proportional to E when τ does not depend on field. For a wire of length L and area A, R = ρL/A and V = IR follow. Copper, with n = 8.5×10²⁸ m⁻³ and τ = 2.5×10⁻¹⁴ s, gives σ ≈ 6.0×10⁷ S/m, close to measured 5.9×10⁷ S/m. Since τ was obtained from that measured value, this is a consistency check. An independent classical estimate of τ still lands within a factor of about two.

items: Phonons: ions vibrate more at higher temperature, so electrons scatter more often and τ falls. Resistivity rises with T.
Impurities and defects: foreign atoms, vacancies or grain boundaries scatter electrons at any temperature. This adds a fixed residual resistivity.

The two add: ρ = ρ_phonon(T) + ρ_residual (Matthiessen's rule). Alloys such as nichrome and constantan have heavy impurity scattering, so high ρ and a weak temperature coefficient; hence heater coils and standard resistors.

sections.h3: What the classical model gets right and what it misses

items: Right — Ohm's law: a linear V–I relation comes out with no extra assumption.
Right — size of σ: computed conductivity of copper, silver and gold lands within a factor of about two of measured values.
Right — Wiedemann–Franz: κ/(σT) is nearly the same constant for all metals, and the electron gas gives this within a factor of about two.
Wrong — heat capacity: equipartition gives (3/2)k_B per electron, so metals should have huge electronic heat capacity. The measured electronic part is far smaller and grows linearly with T.
Wrong — ρ(T): the model predicts ρ ∝ √T because τ ∝ T⁻¹ᐟ². Measured ρ is nearly linear at high T and falls as T⁵ at low T.
Wrong — speed: the model assumes thermal speed near 10⁵ m/s. Electrons move at the Fermi speed, about 10⁶ m/s, even near absolute zero; see 7.2.
Wrong — insulators: every solid contains electrons, yet diamond does not conduct. Allowed bands are needed; see 7.3.

examples.question: Copper has n = 8.5×10²⁸ m⁻³ and τ = 2.5×10⁻¹⁴ s. Take m = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg and e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C. (a) Find σ. (b) A copper wire of cross-section 1.0 mm² carries 2.0 A; find J and v_d.
steps: Cross-check: E = J/σ = 3.35×10⁻² V/m; μ = eτ/m = 4.39×10⁻³ m²/(V·s); v_d = μE = 1.47×10⁻⁴ m/s. Drift is about 0.15 mm per second, far below random speed of about 10⁵ m/s.
examples.answer: For copper, σ ≈ 5.97×10⁷ S/m, J = 2.0×10⁶ A/m² and drift speed is only about 1.5×10⁻⁴ m/s.
examples.check:
n = 8.5e28
tau = 2.5e-14
m = 9.11e-31
e = 1.6e-19
I = 2.0
A = 1.0e-6
sigma = n * e**2 * tau / m
J = I / A
vd = J / (n * e)
print(round(sigma, -5))
print(J)
print(round(vd, 7))

traps: Drift speed is not signal speed or electron speed. v_d ≈ 0.15 mm/s, yet a lamp glows at once because the field spreads along the wire at nearly light speed, and each electron moves randomly at the Fermi speed, about 10⁶ m/s.
Use e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C as a magnitude in σ = ne²τ/m. Substituting −1.6×10⁻¹⁹ gives negative conductivity; σ, ρ and μ are positive.
n must be in m⁻³. A density per cm³ must be multiplied by 10⁶ first, or σ comes out 10⁶ times too small.
τ is mean time between collisions, not mean free path. Mean free path is λ = vτ, where v is fast random speed, never drift speed.

Do not say the classical theory explains resistivity versus temperature. It gets the direction right but the wrong low-temperature power law and the wrong electronic heat capacity; those need quantum statistics and band theory.

quiz.q: List the four assumptions of the classical free electron theory of metals.
quiz.a: Electrons are free between collisions; independent, so electron–electron repulsion is ignored; random, with zero average velocity when no field is applied; colliding with ions after average time τ and losing the velocity gained since the last collision.

quiz.q: Define relaxation time and mobility, and give the unit of each.
quiz.a: Relaxation time τ is average time between two successive collisions, in seconds (≈10⁻¹⁴ s at room temperature). Mobility μ = v_d/E is drift speed per unit field, in m²/(V·s), and μ = eτ/m.

quiz.q: The field keeps pushing electrons, so why does drift velocity settle at a steady value instead of growing?
quiz.a: Each collision randomises velocity and wipes out what the field added since the previous collision. The field acts only for a flight of mean duration τ, so average gain saturates at eEτ/m: electrons just after a collision are slow, those near flight end are fast, and the average stays fixed.

quiz.q: A metal has n = 6.0×10²⁸ m⁻³ and τ = 2.0×10⁻¹⁴ s. Find σ. Take m = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg and e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C.
A silver wire of cross-section 0.50 mm² carries 2.5 A. With n = 5.8×10²⁸ m⁻³, find J and v_d.
Alloying copper with nickel raises resistivity and flattens the resistivity–temperature curve. Explain using τ and Matthiessen's rule.
quiz.a: Scattering rates add: 1/τ = 1/τ_phonon + 1/τ_impurity + 1/τ_defect, so ρ = ρ_phonon(T) + ρ_residual. Impurity atoms add a fixed scattering rate, raising ρ at every temperature. At low temperature the phonon term becomes small and the residual term dominates, so the curve flattens and the temperature coefficient falls.

quiz.q: Classical equipartition predicts electronic heat capacity (3/2)k_B per electron, but metals show a value about a hundred times smaller at room temperature that grows linearly with T. Which assumption fails, and why?
quiz.a: The assumption that every electron can absorb thermal energy of order k_BT like a gas molecule fails. Electrons obey Fermi–Dirac statistics, so states are filled up to the Fermi energy and only the small fraction within about k_BT of it can take thermal energy. That fraction is about T/T_F; with the numerical factor 3, electronic heat capacity is roughly 3T/T_F times the classical value. It is about a hundred times smaller at room temperature and proportional to T; see 7.2.

beyond: Not for the exam. The Matthiessen split — temperature-dependent phonon term plus fixed residual term — is used to specify metals: the residual resistivity ratio, RRR = ρ(273 K)/ρ(4.2 K), grades copper and aluminium for magnets, accelerators and cryogenic cavities. Chip designers fight a related problem, resistivity rise in nanometre-wide copper interconnects from surface and grain-boundary scattering. Search 'Matthiessen rule', 'residual resistivity ratio', 'Fermi surface' and 'copper interconnect size effect' to go further.
